topic: Fundamentals of Linear Algebra: Vectors as Arrows
target_audience: High school students and introductory computer science learners

sections.title: Introduction: What is a Vector?
sections.content: Define a vector not just as a list of numbers, but as a directed segment in 2D space. Explain the 'origin' and 'tip' to help visualize movement.
sections.example: Visualize a robotic arm at the origin (0,0) reaching out to a coordinate (3,2). The vector is the arrow connecting the start to the target.

sections.title: Vector Addition: The Head-to-Tail Rule
sections.content: Introduce vector addition geometrically. Explain that adding two vectors is equivalent to 'walking' the first path, then starting the second path from the end of the first.
sections.example: A cat walks 2 steps East and 3 steps North. Then, it walks another 1 step East and 1 step North. Use a coordinate grid to show the resulting final position (3,4).

sections.title: Scalar Multiplication: Stretching and Flipping
sections.content: Explain how multiplying a vector by a constant (scalar) changes its length. Discuss how negative scalars flip the direction entirely.
sections.example: A video game character jumping: A vector represents the jump strength. Doubling the vector (scalar 2) makes the character jump twice as high; multiplying by -1 makes the character jump downwards.

sections.title: Basis Vectors: The Building Blocks
sections.content: Introduce 'i-hat' (1,0) and 'j-hat' (0,1) as the fundamental basis. Explain that every vector is just a scaled combination of these two pillars.
sections.example: Using Lego bricks: Think of 'i-hat' as a red brick and 'j-hat' as a blue brick. Any coordinate (x, y) is simply x red bricks and y blue bricks stacked together.

sections.title: Summary and Conclusion
sections.content: Synthesize the concepts: Vectors are movements, addition is combining paths, scalars are scaling, and basis vectors are the coordinate system's DNA.
sections.example: Briefly show a navigation app on a phone: '2 miles North, 1 mile East' is effectively a vector addition problem used in real-time GPS tracking.
